Sol.470.(d) Meera is the elder 'Elder' must be replaced with 'eldest'. The definite article 'the' is used before a superlative degree. Hence, 'Meera is the eldest' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.471.(d) in an earlier job, he will never be 'A man' is already mentioned as a subject of this sentence. We cannot use 'he' in the sentence as it becomes the case of superfluousness(not necessary). Therefore, 'he' must be removed from the sentence. Hence, 'in an earlier job, will never be' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.472.(a) that the Monarchy is Article 'the' must be removed. No article is used before the forms of government such as democracy, plutocracy, dictatorship, monarchy. Hence, 'that Monarchy is' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.473.(c) No error . Sol.474.(b) told the rather improbable 'The' must be replaced with 'a'. Article 'the' is used for specific or particular nouns but the 'story' mentioned in the sentence is not specific. Hence, 'told a rather improbable' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.475.(a) although it is urgent. 'Although' must be replaced with 'as / because'. The issue is urgent, that is why discussion on it can not be postponed. Here, we need a connector to show the cause or reason. Hence, 'because it is urgent' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.476.(b) Are you yet 'Yet' must be replaced with 'still'. 'Yet' is used to show contrast between two events. 'Still' is used to show that an action was happening in the past and continuing in the present. Hence, 'Are you still' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.477.(a) very acclaimed 'Very' must be replaced with 'much'. 'Very' is used with present participles(V ing ), not with past participles(V 3 ). Hence, 'much acclaimed' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.478.(b) make it to drink. 'To' must be removed. There are some verbs that take a bare infinitive(without 'to') after them. These are 'make, let, bid, see, watch, observe'. Hence, 'make it drink' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.479.(b) One must do one's duty properly. Sol.480.(b) It is time someone takes Simple Past Tense(Subject + V 2 ) is used after phrases such as 'It is time / It is about time / It is high time'. Therefore, 'takes' will be replaced with 'took(V 2 )'. Hence, 'It is time someone took' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.481.(b) No error. The given sentence is grammatically correct. Sol.482.(c) None than you 'Than' must be replaced with 'but'. The correct phrase is 'none but' or 'none other than', which means 'only'. Hence, 'none but you' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.483.(a) lest you should not 'Lest' is used without 'not'. Hence, 'lest you should' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.484.(d) while the time comes 'While' must be replaced with 'when'. The phrase 'when the time comes' is used to state an action that will be done in the suitable circumstances. Hence, 'when the time comes' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.485.(b) shouldn't we 'Shall we' is the correct question tag for an imperative sentence starting with 'let us'. Hence, 'shall we' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.486.(c) whom I 'Whom' must be replaced with 'which'. 'Whom' is used for a person whereas 'which' is used for things(book). Hence, 'which I' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.487.(a) married happily 'Happily' is an adverb that will be used before the adjective 'married' to modify its meaning. Hence, 'happily married' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.121.(b) have been aching constantly 'Since' is used in present perfect continuous tense to denote an action that started in the past and is still going on. Sol.122.(a) for two months 'For' is used for a definite period of time. For example:- five years, six months, ten days, etc. 'Since' is used to denote a time in the past when something started. questions.question_text: Hardly had the game started ______ the rain began to pour. SSC CGL 14/10/2025 (Shift 3) Sol.1.(a) utmost 'Utmost' means extreme. The given sentence states that due to the fragility of the manuscript, the historian handled it with extreme care. Hence, 'utmost' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.2.(a) into 'Into' is a fixed preposition used with the verb 'delve'. Hence, 'into' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.3.(b) less 'Less' is the comparative form of 'little' and is used here to compare the success of the second attempt with the first. The sentence indicates a reduced level of success in the second attempt. Hence, 'less' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.4.(c) or 'Either…or' is a fixed conjunction pair. Hence, 'or' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.5.(c) whose 'Whose' is a relative adjective used to refer to people or things, indicating possession. In this sentence, the lectures belong to the professor, so 'whose' correctly shows this relationship. Hence, 'whose' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.6.(c) enervate 'Enervate' means to cause (someone) to feel drained of energy or vitality. The given sentence states that the incessant debate began to enervate the enthusiasm of even the most dedicated participants. Hence, 'enervate' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.7.(b) was This sentence is an example of inversion for emphasis, where the auxiliary verb precedes the subject. The subject 'machinery' is singular, so the verb must also be singular. Hence, 'was' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.8.(b) more The word "more" is used here to emphasize that his explanation went beyond merely being confusing, suggesting it was an even greater degree of disorganization and lack of clarity. Hence, "more" is the most appropriate answer. Sol.9.(b) foment The word "foment" means to instigate or stir up (an undesirable or violent sentiment or course of action), which perfectly fits the context of stirring up division. Hence, "foment" is the most appropriate answer. Sol.10.(b) do we have When a sentence begins with a negative adverbial phrase (like 'hardly ever', 'scarcely', 'never', 'seldom', 'rarely'), inversion of the subject and auxiliary verb is required for emphasis. Therefore, 'do we have' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.11.(c) zealotry 'Zealotry' means extreme devotion. The given sentence states that the detective's unwavering commitment to justice often led him to pursue cases with unbridled zealotry. Hence, 'zealotry' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.12.(c) abrade ' Abrade' means to scrape or wear away by friction or erosion. The given sentence states that the constant dripping of water began to abrade the stone, eroding it slowly over centuries. Hence, 'abrade' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.13.(a) fewer 'Fewer' is a comparative degree used with plural countable nouns. Similarly, in the given sentence, 'challenges' is a plural countable noun. Hence, 'fewer' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.14.(c) however 'However' is an adverb used to introduce a statement that contrasts with or contradicts something that has been said previously. Here, it presents a contrast between the promise of streamlined operations and complex implementation. Hence, 'however' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.15.(a) sustained 'Sustained' means to suffer (something unpleasant, especially an injury, a defeat, or a loss). The given sentence states that the city would have sustained significant damage from the tsunami if not for the early warning system. Hence, 'sustained' Sol.16.(d) motivates In the given sentence, 'the constant criticism' is a singular subject that will take 'motivates' as a singular verb. Hence, 'motivates' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.17.(a) at 'At' is a fixed preposition used with 'adept'. Hence, 'at' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.18.(d) arrived If two actions took place in the past then the 1st action must be in the Past perfect tense(Had + V3) and the 2nd action must be in the Simple Past tense(V 2 ). In the given sentence, 'evacuation' is the 1st action & 'arrival' is the 2nd action. Hence, 'arrived(V 2 )' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.19.(b) which "Which" is a relative pronoun used to introduce a non-restrictive clause that refers to things or animals. In this case, "which" refers back to "proposals." Hence, 'which' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.20.(c) had If a sentence starts with a negative word (hardly / barely / scarcely / rarely / no sooner / not only / never / little), the correct grammatical structure is 'Negative word + Helping verb + Subject + Main Verb'. The sentence describes an action completed before another past action, so it requires Past Perfect Tense (had + V3). Hence, 'had' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.21.(a) Contradictory The word 'contradictory' means opposite or inconsistent with something else. The sentence suggests that the scientist's conclusions did not agree with the data in the report. Hence, 'Contradictory' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.22.(c) than 'No sooner-than' is the fixed conjunction pair. Hence, 'than' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.23.(a) In spite of "In spite of" is a prepositional phrase meaning "despite" or "regardless of." It correctly conveys a contrast between being warned and proceeding with the action. Hence, "In spite of" is the most appropriate answer.

questions.question_text: Both the criminals were cruel and ______. Sol.258.(a) through; along 'Along' means by the side of something such as a road or river. 'Through' is used to indicate movement from one side to another. The given sentence states that he walked through the park and later strolled along the riverbank. Hence, 'through; along' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.259.(d) to undertake Infinitive(to + V 1 ) is used after the verb 'decide'. Hence, 'to undertake(V 1 )' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.260.(b) to speak Infinitive (to + V 1 ) is used after the verb 'hope'. Hence, 'to speak(V 1 )' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.261.(c) otherwise 'Otherwise' is used to tell the consequences of not following certain instructions. Similarly, the given sentence states that there would have been consequences if she did not follow the instructions meticulously. Hence, 'otherwise' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.262.(a) will find The given sentence is an example of the first conditional sentence and 'If + simple present tense, … will + V 1 ' is the correct grammatical structure for it. Hence, 'will find(V 1 )' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.263.(c) A; the 'Top' mentioned in the given sentence is specific and we generally use the definite article 'the' before a specific noun. The two girls are not specified in the sentence, therefore article 'the' cannot be used before the noun 'team'. 'Team' starts with a consonant sound, therefore article 'a' will be used. Hence, 'A; the' is the most appropriate answer.

questions.question_text: The issue of fairness, which remained, was for consideration at the hearing to _________ the scheme. Sol.583.(b) Has been The given sentence is an example of present perfect continuous tense. As we generally use the present perfect continuous tense to talk about actions and states that began in the past and are still continuing at the time of speaking. Hence, 'has been' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.584.(a) More The word 'more' is used to indicate a greater quantity or number. The given sentence states that I am sorry that I was unable to see more of you over the summer. Hence, 'more' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.585.(b) Lying Lying means 'to lie' (put yourself in a horizontal or resting position). The given sentence states that John rushed to the spot and saw his wife and kid lying on the road. Hence, 'lying' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.586.(c) Heard 'Heard' means to listen or pay attention to. The given sentence states that today I received a letter. Finally, I heard back from him. Hence, 'heard' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.587.(d) Accompany 'Accompany' means to go somewhere with someone. The given sentence states that women accompany their male relatives to the battlefield for the purpose of tending the wounded and carrying away the dead. Hence, 'Accompany' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.588.(b) Bruise 'Bruise' means an injury or mark where the skin has not been broken but is darker in colour. The given sentence states that the most common sports injury is a bruise. Hence, 'Bruise' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.589.(a) Breathable 'Breathable clothes' means clothes from which air can pass through easily. The given sentence states that since the temperatures can soar in summer, choose clothing that is lightweight and breathable. Hence, 'Breathable' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.590.(c) Whimsical 'Whimsical' means unusual and strange in a way that might be funny or annoying.The given sentence states that this whimsical piece of mischief by his brother brought a quiet laugh from David. Hence, 'Whimsical' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.591.(a) his mouth like Preposition 'like' is generally used to establish a relationship between nouns, pronouns, or phrases with other words in a sentence. In this case, "like" is showing a comparison between two things - the layering of regret and the feeling or state of Drupad's mouth. Hence, 'his mouth like' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.592.(d) Supine 'Supine' means a person lying face upward. The given sentence states that during treatment, patients lay supine on the treatment couch for around 3 hrs. Hence, 'Supine' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.593.(d) administered/middle 'Administered' means to control the situation, operation or arrangement of something. The given sentence states that If the anesthesia is not administered properly, he might wake up in the middle of the surgery. Hence , 'administered/middle' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.594.(c) adaptive 'Adaptive' means having an ability to change to suit changing conditions.The given sentence states that societies need to develop highly adaptive behavioural rules for survival. Hence, 'adaptive' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.595.(a) Implacable 'Implacable' means refusing to change and showing no forgiveness or mercy. The given sentence states that the man who is supposed to be protecting them is somehow their fiercest and most implacable enemy. Hence, 'implacable' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.596.(b) Temperance 'Temperance' means moderation in action, thought, or feeling. The given sentence states that before about 1830, temperance sermons, tracts and addresses routinely broached female intemperance. Hence,'Temperance' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.597.(d) Garner 'Garner' means to gather or collect. The given sentence states that according to the politician, using vulgar language to garner votes is not something he will endorse. Hence, 'Garner' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.598.(c) Unearth 'Unearth' means to discover. The given sentence states that I was really hoping to unearth a decent movie this time, and I came up with an undisputed classic. Hence, 'unearth' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.599.(d) To the The phrase 'To the' is generally used to indicate movement or transition from one place or position to another. Hence, 'to the' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.600.(a) Concentrate 'Concentrate' means to focus all one's attention on a particular object or activity. The given sentence states that the sedative effect of the drugs impairs people's ability to pay attention and concentrate. Hence, 'Concentrate' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.601.(b) Over The phrase 'All over' means everywhere. The given sentence states that she kept pictures of her parents all over the house. Hence, 'Over' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.602.(c) When it 'When' functions as a subordinating conjunction. As a subordinating conjunction, 'when' introduces a dependent clause that provides additional information about the timing or condition of the main clause. It establishes a relationship between the two clauses. Hence, 'When it' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.603.(d) least The phrase "last but not least" is a commonly used expression indicating that something is mentioned as the final item on a list, but it is not less important than the previous ones. Hence, 'least' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.604.(b) Ameliorate 'Ameliorate' means to improve or make something better. The given sentence states that Obesity is also a progressive condition, unlike anorexia nervosa, which tends to ameliorate with age. Hence, 'ameliorate' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.605.(c) Peripheral 'Peripheral' refers to something that is situated at the edge or boundary of something. The given sentence states that Sitting at the computer I saw something large and dark fall past my peripheral vision followed by a dull thwack. Hence, 'peripheral' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.606.(d) Exigent 'Exigent' means pressing, urgent, or requiring immediate action or attention. The given sentence states that In my view, this falls within the exception permitting warrantless seizure in exigent circumstances. Hence, 'exigent' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.607.(b) innocuous 'Innocuous' means not meant to cause harm or upset somebody. The given sentence states that the question is why an innocuous Hollywood film should provoke such a hostile reaction. Hence, 'innocuous' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.608.(b) anomaly 'Anomaly' means deviation from the normal or common form. The given sentence states that fetal anomaly screening uses ultrasound scanning to find certain abnormalities in the baby. Hence, 'anomaly' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.609.(d) alleviate 'Alleviate' means to make something less severe. The given sentence states that people afflicted with the itchy skin condition used stinky coal tar derivatives to alleviate their symptoms. Hence, 'alleviate' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.610.(b) Counterproductive "Counterproductive" means that it is not achieving the desired results and is actually hindering progress or success. The given sentence states that - This initiative has been sharply criticised as grossly inefficient and counterproductive. Hence, 'counterproductive' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.611.(c) Condemn 'Forgive' means to pardon or show mercy. The given sentence states that We cannot forgive a religion or a political party that ignores the rights of half the human race. Hence, 'Forgive' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.612.(c) Lewd 'Lewd' means obscene, vulgar. The given sentence states that - The duke had capacity, but his life was so lewd that what influence he had upon the king was for evil. Sol.613.(b) terror 'Terror' means the feeling of strong fear.The given sentence states that disturbing emotions begin to build into fear, and then terror. Hence, 'terror' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.614.(d) seemed The main clause (having the verb 'bowed') is already given in past tense and is connected to the second clause using the conjunction 'but'. So, the second clause will also be written in past tense. Hence, 'seemed' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.615.(c) samples The phrase 'air samples' means a small amount of air that is collected for testing pollutants in the air. The given sentence states that the researchers took air samples from the room every five minutes to rule out the possibility of a new virus. Hence, 'samples' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.616.(b) Holy 'Holy' means sacred or associated with divinity or religious significance. The given sentence states that The priest puts some holy water on the child's head. Hence, 'holy' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.617.(b) Effort 'Effort' means the act of exerting energy or taking action to accomplish something. The given sentence states that all the companies make an effort to be seen and heard within communities. Hence, 'effort' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.618.(b) Mundane 'Mundane' means lacking excitement or interest. The given sentence states that Jacqueline represents retirement as the final result of a long course of dissatisfaction with mundane life. Hence, 'mundane' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.619.(c) improves 'Improve' means to raise to a better condition. The given sentence states that strength training is useful as it avoids large increases in breathing rate and improves muscle strength. Hence, 'improves' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.620.(c) walk The given sentence states that he gave the horse enough room to walk away from the wagon. Hence, 'walk' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.621.(c) Aside 'Aside from' is a phrase used to mean 'apart from' or 'except for'. It indicates that lions are the primary natural predators of elephants, with the exception of humans. Hence, 'aside' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.622.(d) Thrown 'Thrown' means to send suddenly into a particular state or condition. The given sentence states that -If she hadn't thrown her cell phone on the bed, she could have called him. Hence, 'thrown' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.623.(b) danger 'Danger' means something or someone that may harm you. The given sentence states that fear evolved over millions of years to protect us from danger. Hence, 'danger' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.624.(c) jell 'Jell' means to form or develop into something more concrete or workable. The given sentence states that the plan began to jell once we all met to discuss. Hence, 'jell' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.625.(b) Cloud 'Cloud' means to obscure or hinder clear thinking or judgment. The given sentence states that I am just saying that maybe you are letting emotion cloud your better judgment right now. Hence, 'cloud' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.626.(d) Habit 'Habit' refers to a regular or repeated behavior that someone has developed. The given sentence states that His habit of smoking in restaurants created a lot of issues in New York. Hence, 'habit' is the most appropriate answer.

SET - 3 [Q .11. to Q .15.] The symbiotic relationship between flowering plants and their pollinators is a cornerstone of global biodiversity and ecosystem stability. Pollinators, primarily insects like bees, butterflies, and moths, but also birds and bats, play a crucial role in the reproduction of over 80% of the world's flowering plants, including many food crops essential for human sustenance. As these animals visit flowers to feed on nectar or pollen, they inadvertently transfer pollen grains from one flower to another, enabling fertilization. This intricate dance has evolved over millions of years, leading to highly specialized adaptations in both plants and pollinators. For instance, some flowers have evolved specific shapes, colors, or scents to attract particular pollinators, while pollinators have developed specialized mouthparts or behaviors to access the rewards offered by these flowers. However, this vital relationship is under severe threat from various anthropogenic factors. Habitat loss due to urbanization and agriculture, pesticide use (especially neonicotinoids), climate change altering bloom times, and the spread of diseases and invasive species are collectively contributing to a dramatic decline in pollinator populations worldwide. The consequences of this decline are far-reaching. Beyond the ecological impact on wild plant reproduction, there are significant economic implications for agriculture. Many fruits, vegetables, and nuts rely heavily on animal pollination, and a reduction in pollinator services can lead to lower yields, reduced quality, and increased food costs. Scientists are actively researching solutions, from promoting pollinator-friendly farming practices and creating urban pollinator gardens to developing less harmful pest management strategies and conserving natural habitats. Understanding and protecting these unsung heroes of our ecosystems is paramount for food security and the health of our planet. SSC CGL 12/09/2025 (Shift 3)

SET - 4 [Q .16. to Q .20.] The air in the kitchen was thick with unspoken words, heavier than the simmering stew on the hob. Fifteen-year-old Liam stared at his phone, thumb scrolling endlessly, while his mother, Sarah, meticulously arranged vegetables on a chopping board, each slice a deliberate effort to avoid eye contact. It had been like this for weeks, ever since the text message, the one that splintered their comfortable silence. "Why can't you just talk to me?" Sarah's voice was low, strained, finally breaking the quiet. Liam flinched, his jaw tightening. "There's nothing to talk about." A familiar, brick-wall response. He knew what she wanted - an explanation for his sudden withdrawal, the late nights, the abrupt change in his friend group. But how could he explain the pressure, the constant barrage of judgment from online 'friends' he barely knew, the relentless need to project an image of effortless cool ? He remembered the first time he'd felt the sting of exclusion - a meme, shared widely in his class group chat, subtly mocking his older brother's passion for chess. He'd laughed along, a hollow, uncomfortable sound, desperate to fit in. Then came the 'dares,' escalating from minor pranks to something that made his stomach clench with fear. He'd tried to pull away, to mute the notifications, but the fear of being truly alone, ostracized from the only social circle he currently had, was suffocating. His old friends, the ones he'd shared genuine laughter with, felt distant, almost alien now. Sarah sighed, a sound of profound weariness. "Liam, I see you. I see you pulling away, shutting down. Whatever it is, we can face it together." He heard the tremor in her voice, the genuine concern, but a powerful knot of shame and fear kept his lips sealed. He glanced up, his eyes meeting hers for a fleeting second - a cavern of unspoken anxiety reflected in his gaze before he retreated back behind the glow of his screen, the silent battle raging on.

SET - 5 [Q .21. to Q .25.] The perennial discussion surrounding the value of a liberal arts education in a technologically driven world often pits practical, vocational training against broader intellectual development. Critics argue that in an era demanding specialized skills and immediate job readiness, degrees in fields like philosophy, literature, or history are impractical and fail to equip graduates for the modern workforce. They emphasize the need for STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields, which directly contribute to economic growth and offer clearer career paths with higher earning potential, asserting that a focus on specific, marketable skills is the most efficient route to professional success. However, proponents of a liberal arts education contend that its value lies precisely in its capacity to cultivate adaptable, critical thinkers-qualities that are increasingly vital in a rapidly changing global landscape. Instead of narrowly focusing on 'what to think,' a liberal arts curriculum teaches 'how to think.' It exposes students to a wide range of disciplines, fostering intellectual curiosity, analytical reasoning, effective communication, and problem-solving abilities that transcend specific industries or technologies. Graduates learn to interpret complex information, articulate persuasive arguments, understand diverse cultural contexts, and approach challenges from multiple perspectives-skills that are foundational for leadership, innovation, and civic engagement. In a world where automation and AI are poised to transform many specialized jobs, the uniquely human capacities developed through a liberal arts education-creativity, ethical reasoning, empathy, and holistic understanding -become more, not less, valuable. Employers increasingly seek individuals who can adapt to new challenges, collaborate effectively, and contribute to organizational culture, rather than merely possessing a narrow technical skill set that might quickly become obsolete. Therefore, a liberal arts education, far from being impractical, provides a robust intellectual toolkit that prepares individuals not just for a first job, but for a lifetime of learning, career transitions, and meaningful contributions to society.

A few decades ago, printed books and newspapers were the primary sources of information and leisure reading. While this shift has made reading more convenient, it has also raised concerns about declining attention spans and reduced comprehension. Printed books, on the other hand, encourage focus and retention through a more immersive experience. Despite these concerns, digital reading has several undeniable advantages. Moreover, digital platforms promote environmental sustainability by reducing paper consumption. However, some educators argue that an overreliance on screens can cause eye strain, fatigue, and even disrupt sleep patterns due to prolonged exposure to blue light. Ultimately, the debate between digital and print reading is not about choosing one over the other, but about achieving balance. Readers can enjoy the convenience of technology while still preserving the depth of traditional reading. By practising mindful reading-whether on paper or screen-individuals can ensure that technology enhances rather than weakens their intellectual engagement. SSC CGL 13/09/2025 (Shift 3)

They argue that every technological revolution-printing press, calculator, or computer-has similarly redefined intelligence rather than diminished it. The central challenge, therefore, is not resisting technology but using it judiciously-balancing cognitive independence with technological assistance. The future of human intellect will likely depend on how effectively individuals cultivate mindfulness in an age of mental automation.

Philosophers from Lao Tzu to Wittgenstein have observed that language, though powerful, often fractures experience into fragments that silence alone can reconcile. True understanding, therefore, may not always lie in articulation but in the spaces between words-the pauses that lend speech its meaning. Moreover, silence carries moral and emotional weight. It can soothe or wound, liberate or oppress. The silence of complicity sustains injustice, while the silence of contemplation heals. In learning to listen-to others, to nature, to ourselves-we recover a dimension of awareness long buried beneath the noise of modern life. Silence, then, is not absence but essence: the quiet pulse beneath the surface of existence that restores depth to being.

It promises objectivity, progress, and mastery over nature, yet it simultaneously engenders profound ethical dilemmas. The relentless pursuit of innovation often outpaces moral reflection, leaving humanity to confront consequences it is ill-prepared to manage. From genetic modification to artificial intelligence, scientific advancement expands the boundaries of what can be done, while offering little guidance on what should be done. This widening gap between capability and conscience underscores the need for an ethical framework that evolves in tandem with discovery. Historically, science has been regarded as a neutral enterprise-its value determined by human application. However, this notion of neutrality is increasingly untenable in a world where data, algorithms, and biotechnologies directly shape social realities. The scientist no longer functions solely as an observer but as an active agent of transformation, capable of altering both the environment and the human condition itself. Consequently, the question of responsibility becomes inseparable from the act of inquiry. Ethics, then, cannot remain external to science; it must be integrated within its very methodology. The development of nuclear weapons, surveillance technologies, and environmental exploitation has demonstrated that knowledge divorced from moral accountability leads to existential peril. In this sense, ethical deliberation is not an impediment to progress but its precondition. The challenge lies in reconciling the empirical rigor of science with the normative demands of ethics -an endeavor that requires humility, dialogue, and an awareness of science's sociopolitical embeddedness. To imagine science as detached from values is to ignore the historical record of how power and ideology have influenced research agendas, from colonial anthropology to corporate-funded pharmacology. In the twenty first century, as humanity stands at the threshold of genetic redesign and machine consciousness, the integration of ethical reasoning into scientific practice is no longer optional but essential. The true measure of scientific progress will thus depend not merely on discovery, but on discernment-on our collective ability to wield knowledge without surrendering wisdom. questions.question_text: The author's tone in the passage can best be described as- SET - 14 [Q .66. to Q .70.] India, a nation celebrated for its vibrant diversity and economic aspirations, concurrently navigates a labyrinth of persistent social challenges that often impede its journey towards genuinely inclusive development. While significant economic growth has lifted millions out of poverty, the benefits have not been uniformly distributed, leading to widening disparities. The pervasive issue of inequality is multi-dimensional, extending beyond mere income gaps to encompass unequal access to quality education, healthcare, and digital literacy. The historical stratification of society, particularly the enduring influence of the caste system, continues to perpetuate disadvantages for certain communities, despite constitutional provisions for affirmative action. Gender inequality remains another formidable barrier. Women, though increasingly visible in public life, frequently confront systemic discrimination, gender-based violence, and a significant wage gap. Their participation in the formal workforce, while growing, is still considerably lower than men's, reflecting deeply entrenched patriarchal norms that limit opportunities and autonomy. Moreover, the strain on public health infrastructure is acute. India battles a dual burden of communicable and non - communicable diseases. Malnutrition and a lack of adequate sanitation, especially in rural and urban slum areas, contribute to high rates of infant mortality and morbidity. The recent pandemic starkly exposed the vulnerabilities of an overburdened healthcare system, underscoring the urgent need for greater investment and equitable distribution of medical resources. Simultaneously, environmental degradation poses an existential threat, particularly to vulnerable populations. Rapid industrialization and urban sprawl have led to alarming levels of air and water pollution, exacerbating respiratory illnesses and contaminating vital water sources. Deforestation contributes to ecological imbalances and climate change impacts, such as extreme weather events, which disproportionately affect agricultural communities and those reliant on natural resources. These issues are interconnected, forming a vicious cycle where poverty intensifies environmental vulnerability, and environmental harm further entrenches poverty and ill-health. Addressing these challenges necessitates a holistic approach: strengthening governance, promoting ethical leadership, fostering robust public-private partnerships, and, crucially, empowering citizens through education and genuine participation. It demands a commitment to fostering a society where progress is measured not just by economic indicators, but by the well-being, equity, and dignity afforded to every single individual. Originality, often romanticized as the spark of divine inspiration, is revered as the lifeblood of artistic and intellectual progress. The original creator, unshackled by precedent, is celebrated as a pioneer who redefines the boundaries of the possible. Yet, imitation-frequently dismissed as parasitic mimicry - possesses its own quiet genius. To imitate with discernment is to study the anatomy of excellence; it is the apprenticeship through which mastery often gestates. The Renaissance, after all, flourished not through isolation but through reinterpretation. However, the fetishization of originality in modern culture risks estranging creators from the continuum of human knowledge. Every so-called innovation is, in essence, an echo refracted through time-an evolution rather than an eruption. Conversely, blind imitation breeds stagnation, where the act of creation devolves into mechanical repetition devoid of insight. The truth lies in equilibrium: originality must converse with tradition even as it challenges it. The most profound works, whether in art, science, or thought, emerge not from rebellion alone but from synthesis - where imitation provides the scaffolding and originality raises the edifice. In this delicate dialectic, creativity becomes less an act of invention and more an act of intelligent remembrance, where the past is neither idolized nor ignored but transmuted into something enduringly new.

SET - 18 [Q .86. to Q .90.] Industrialization in colonial India represented a paradox of progress-an appearance of modernization concealing deep economic subordination. The British industrial revolution, powered by technological innovation and capitalist expansion, found in India both a vast market and a limitless source of raw materials. Yet, rather than fostering indigenous industrial growth, colonial policies deliberately stifled it. India, once renowned for its textile craftsmanship, saw its thriving handloom sector dismantled through a combination of tariff manipulation, import domination, and the flooding of British-manufactured goods. The railways, often celebrated as symbols of modernization, primarily served the colonial purpose of resource extraction and troop movement rather than national integration. Similarly, irrigation and infrastructure projects were designed less for agricultural welfare and more for enhancing revenue collection and export efficiency. The colonial economy thus functioned as an appendage to British industry - structured to benefit the metropolis while impoverishing the colony. The decline of local industries displaced artisans and created widespread unemployment, while the agrarian population faced mounting land revenue demands and indebtedness. The resulting deindustrialization transformed India from a producer of finished goods to a supplier of raw materials like cotton, jute, and indigo. Even the emergence of Indian entrepreneurs in the late nineteenth century occurred within a highly restrictive framework that favored British capital. Industrial growth was permitted only when it aligned with imperial interests, reinforcing dependency rather than self-sufficiency. This economic pattern laid the foundation for structural inequalities that persisted long after independence. The rhetoric of 'development' during colonial rule thus masked an exploitative design, where progress was measured not by Indian prosperity but by the profitability of the empire. SET - 19 [Q .91. to Q .95.] Air pollution has emerged as one of the gravest environmental challenges of the 21st century, particularly in rapidly urbanising regions of Asia and Africa. While economic expansion and urban growth have lifted millions out of poverty, they have also intensified the concentration of harmful pollutants such as particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and ground-level ozone. Unlike the visible soot and smog of the industrial revolution, today's pollution is more insidious, operating at a microscopic level and silently undermining human health and ecological stability. According to global health reports, prolonged exposure to fine particulate matter can cause chronic respiratory illnesses, cardiovascular disorders, and even premature death. Yet, despite the well-documented consequences, policy responses often remain fragmented and reactive. A systematic solution to the air quality crisis must begin with comprehensive monitoring. Many cities lack reliable, real-time data, making it difficult to identify pollution hotspots or enforce emission norms effectively. Expanding the network of air quality sensors and integrating satellite-based data can create a more accurate picture of pollution dynamics. This data-driven approach would allow authorities to implement targeted interventions rather than blanket restrictions. Secondly, the transportation sector demands structural reform. Vehicular emissions constitute a major share of urban pollution. Promoting electric mobility through subsidies, expanding public transport, and improving last-mile connectivity can significantly cut tailpipe emissions. Simultaneously, strict inspection and maintenance regimes for older vehicles should be enforced to phase out the most polluting fleets. Industrial emissions require equal attention. Establishing green industrial corridors, adopting cleaner production technologies, and introducing market-based mechanisms such as emission trading schemes can reduce the carbon and pollution footprint of manufacturing zones. Additionally, transitioning from coal to renewable energy sources like solar, wind, and bioenergy can gradually decouple economic growth from environmental harm. At the community level, awareness and behavioural change are indispensable. Citizens can contribute by reducing household waste burning, conserving energy, and supporting local green initiatives. Schools and civic bodies must incorporate environmental education to instil sustainable habits early on. Moreover, coordinated regional action is vital because air pollution does not respect administrative boundaries. Countries sharing airsheds-such as India, Bangladesh, and Nepal-must collaborate on emission inventories, early warning systems, and technology exchange. In essence, clean air cannot be achieved through isolated efforts or temporary bans. It demands an integrated policy framework that combines technology, governance, public participation, and transnational cooperation. The air we breathe is a shared resource, and its protection requires a collective commitment to sustainability, accountability, and scientific precision.

SET - 20 [Q .96. to Q .100.] In an era dominated by digital interconnectivity, the concept of 'truth' has undergone a profound transformation. Once anchored in verifiable facts and shared understanding, it now often floats within fragmented online realities shaped by algorithms and personal biases. The democratization of information-while seemingly empowering - has paradoxically made distinguishing fact from fiction increasingly difficult. Social media platforms, under the guise of free expression, amplify voices not by credibility but by engagement metrics. As a result, emotional intensity often outweighs evidence, and virality substitutes for validity. The architecture of digital discourse rewards polarization; outrage generates clicks, and clicks generate profit. Consequently, misinformation thrives, spreading faster than verified facts. The modern individual, inundated by competing narratives, gravitates toward information that aligns with pre-existing beliefs-a psychological phenomenon known as confirmation bias. This creates parallel realities where objective truth becomes secondary to ideological comfort. News consumers are no longer passive recipients but active participants in shaping the narratives they wish to believe. However, the problem is not technology itself but our uncritical dependence on it. Search engines and feeds, optimized for personalization, narrow our exposure to diverse perspectives. True digital literacy, therefore, lies not in constant connectivity but in critical awareness - questioning sources, examining intent, and embracing discomfort in confronting opposing viewpoints. Only through such self-reflection can individuals reclaim the integrity of truth in an age designed to distort it. SSC CGL 18/09/2025 (Shift 2)

SET - 21 [Q .101. to Q .105.] In an era defined by relentless technological acceleration, the concept of time has undergone a profound transformation. What was once a natural rhythm, guided by the alternation of day and night, has become an economic commodity subject to precision, measurement, and monetization. The Industrial Revolution marked the first decisive shift, synchronizing human activity with the ticking of the clock. Factory whistles replaced the crow of the rooster, and punctuality became a moral virtue. In the digital age, this commodification has intensified. Every moment is tracked, categorized, and optimized-an invisible currency traded in the global marketplace of attention. Time management is no longer a simple skill but an ideological expectation that governs modern life. The lexicon of efficiency has infiltrated both professional and personal spheres, equating speed with intelligence and busyness with value. Leisure, once considered restorative, is now subtly framed as unproductive or even wasteful. The pressure to constantly perform, respond, and produce has eroded the capacity for stillness. Humanity's obsession with saving time paradoxically ensures that there is never enough of it. This mechanized relationship with time breeds a deep psychological alienation. The more individuals attempt to master time, the more subservient they become to its relentless quantification. Pre-industrial societies perceived time as cyclical and collective, attuned to the organic patterns of nature-the harvest, the tide, the moon. Time flowed with life, not against it. Today, however, the digital clock abstracts time from lived experience, rendering it uniform, fragmented, and detached from meaning. The day becomes a sequence of scheduled obligations rather than an unfolding of moments. The age of hyper-connectivity has further distorted temporal perception. Instant communication fosters impatience; delayed responses evoke anxiety. The constant flow of notifications creates an illusion of perpetual urgency, where silence feels like a void that must be filled. This culture of immediacy undermines contemplation and depth. As philosopher Byung-Chul Han observes, 'the contemplative pause' - once essential to creativity and understanding - is vanishing. Without it, thought becomes shallow, and relationships transactional. To reclaim agency over time, humanity must reimagine it not as a resource to be spent but as a medium through which meaning, connection, and reflection emerge. Time, in its richest sense, is not a race against the clock but an art of presence - an act of inhabiting each moment fully. Only by learning to dwell, rather than to hurry, can we recover the lost harmony between time, technology, and the self.

SET - 22 [Q .106. to Q .110.] Justice and equality, though often invoked together, are distinct yet interdependent ideals that form the backbone of any democratic society. Justice concerns itself with fairness ensuring that individuals receive what they are due, based on merit, need, or equity. Equality, on the other hand, demands that all individuals be treated the same, without discrimination or privilege. However, absolute equality can sometimes undermine justice, just as rigid notions of justice may perpetuate inequality. For instance, providing identical resources to students from vastly different socio-economic backgrounds may appear equal but fails to be just, as it ignores contextual disadvantages. Hence, modern social theorists argue for 'equity' - a dynamic balance that considers differences without abandoning fairness. Philosophers from Aristotle to Rawls have grappled with this tension. Aristotle viewed justice as giving each person their due, emphasizing proportional fairness rather than sameness. Centuries later, John Rawls introduced the 'veil of ignorance' a thought experiment suggesting that just principles are those chosen without knowing one's social status. His theory underscored that true fairness must protect the least advantaged, not merely maintain formal equality. However, translating such philosophical ideals into public policy is rarely straightforward. Bureaucratic systems often reduce nuanced principles into rigid procedures, where equality is measured by uniform rules rather than outcomes. The digital age adds another layer to this debate. Algorithms used in hiring, lending, or law enforcement claim objectivity but often reproduce existing biases encoded in data. A recruitment system that screens candidates purely on 'neutral' data may still discriminate against marginalized groups, revealing how equality in process does not always yield justice in result. Therefore, achieving a just society demands constant reflection - to move beyond mechanical equality and toward fairness rooted in empathy, adaptability, and moral imagination.

SET - 23 [Q .111. to Q .115.] In an age characterized by constant connection and excessive information, the idea of being alone has become both rare and vital. Rather than being the same as loneliness, solitude signifies a mindful retreat-a purposeful effort to recover mental clarity and inner calm. Throughout history, thinkers, writers, and inventors have sought time in seclusion as a means for profound thought and invention. In solitude, the mind is free from social expectations, allowing ideas to form in their pure and unfiltered state. Yet today, solitude is often misunderstood, seen as unproductive or antisocial. The dominance of digital interaction has weakened our ability to spend time alone, replacing self-reflection with continuous stimulation. Messages, feeds, and the reward loop of online approval sustain a cycle of distraction that divides focus and reduces awareness. On a psychological level, being alone provides a moment for emotional balance. It allows people to interpret their experiences without the pressure of comparison or approval. Scientific studies indicate that deliberate solitude activates the brain's resting network, connected to memory, identity, and imagination. Interestingly, individuals who regularly spend time alone often show stronger empathy and social connection, as they engage with others from a stable sense of self rather than dependence. Culturally, however, the glorification of busyness and constant activity has made solitude seem unusual. Communities that measure value by output tend to ignore the restorative role of stillness. Regaining solitude, therefore, requires both structural and personal adjustments-defining achievement not only by what one does but also by what one understands. True solitude is not withdrawal, but integration: a reunion with one's own thoughts and purpose. In the quiet of being alone, one does not avoid the world but learns to face it with renewed insight.

SET - 25 [Q .121. to Q .125.] In the digital age, personal data has become one of the most valuable commodities, shaping how businesses, governments, and individuals interact. Every online search, social media post, and mobile transaction contributes to a vast ecosystem of data collection and analysis. Tech giants employ sophisticated algorithms to track user preferences, predict behavior, and deliver personalized advertisements that seem almost intuitive. While this data-driven world enhances convenience and efficiency, it simultaneously exposes individuals to unprecedented privacy risks. The boundaries between public and private life are blurring as personal information becomes a tradable asset, often exchanged without informed consent. Governments argue that surveillance technologies are essential for national security and public safety, yet the same tools can be misused to monitor citizens, suppress dissent, or manipulate elections. Data breaches and unauthorized access to confidential information have become alarmingly frequent, eroding public trust in digital institutions. In many cases, users agree to complex privacy policies they barely read, granting corporations sweeping rights over their data in exchange for 'free' services. This imbalance of power raises critical ethical questions: Who truly owns personal data? How much control should individuals retain over their digital footprints? Addressing these concerns requires a multi-dimensional approach. Stronger data protection laws, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), aim to empower users by ensuring transparency and consent. Similarly, initiatives in India like the Digital Personal Data Protection Act seek to safeguard citizens' privacy while enabling responsible innovation. However, legislation alone cannot solve the problem. Public awareness, ethical corporate behavior, and the promotion of digital literacy are equally vital. As technology continues to evolve-from facial recognition to artificial intelligence-the ethical use of data will determine the future of digital democracy. Ultimately, privacy in the 21st century is not just a legal right but a fundamental expression of personal autonomy, dignity, and freedom in an interconnected world

SET - 26 [Q .126. to Q .130.] Deep beneath the ocean's surface lies one of the least explored frontiers on Earth - the abyssal plain. Stretching across vast regions of the seabed, these flat, dark expanses are home to an array of organisms uniquely adapted to conditions of crushing pressure, perpetual darkness, and scarce food supply. Life here thrives not on sunlight but on chemical energy derived from hydrothermal vents, where mineral-rich fluids gush from the Earth's crust. Around these vents, chemosynthetic bacteria form the foundation of an entire ecosystem, sustaining giant tube worms, blind shrimp, and specialised crabs. The discovery of these vent-based ecosystems in the late 20th century revolutionised our understanding of life itself, challenging the long-held notion that sunlight was essential for biological productivity. The study of such organisms has also deepened scientific insight into possible extraterrestrial life, particularly on icy moons like Europa and Enceladus, where similar energy sources may exist beneath frozen crusts. Yet, the growing interest in deep-sea mining threatens to disturb these fragile habitats. Extraction of minerals such as cobalt, nickel, and rare earth elements could irreversibly damage ecosystems that have taken millennia to evolve. Scientists urge that conservation and research must precede exploitation, ensuring that curiosity does not turn into destruction.

SET - 28 [Q .136. to Q .140.] Nutrition is the process by which living organisms obtain the food necessary for growth, metabolism, and other vital functions. It encompasses a vast array of biochemical and physiological processes, beginning with ingestion and culminating in the assimilation of nutrients at the cellular level. Macronutrients -carbohydrates, proteins, and fats -are required in larger quantities as they provide the bulk of energy and building blocks for bodily structures. Carbohydrates are the body's primary energy source, proteins are crucial for tissue repair and enzyme production, while fats are essential for hormone production, nutrient absorption, and organ protection. Micronutrients, though needed in smaller amounts, are equally indispensable. These include vitamins and minerals, which play pivotal roles in myriad enzymatic reactions, immune function, and overall cellular health. For instance, Vitamin C is vital for collagen synthesis and immune support, while iron is central to oxygen transport in the blood. A deficiency in any micronutrient can lead to specific health issues, ranging from mild impairments to severe diseases. The concept of a "balanced diet" is foundational to good nutrition, advocating for a diverse intake of foods from all major food groups to ensure adequate provision of both macronutrients and micronutrients. However, modern dietary patterns, often characterized by highly processed foods, excessive sugar, and unhealthy fats, frequently deviate from this ideal. These imbalances contribute significantly to the global burden of non-communicable diseases, such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Understanding the intricate relationship between diet and health empowers individuals to make informed choices, fostering well-being and preventing chronic illness. Educating the public on nutritional science is, therefore, a crucial public health endeavour. SSC CGL 22/09/2025 (Shift 2)

SET - 32 [Q .156. to Q .160.] The concept of environmental stewardship encompasses more than mere conservation; it represents a proactive commitment to sustaining the biosphere through ethical engagement, scientific insight, and social responsibility. Ecosystems, as intricate networks of interdependent species and abiotic factors, demonstrate that ecological stability is contingent upon balance rather than domination. Historically, human societies that harmonized their activities with natural rhythms-through agrarian practices, sacred groves, or community-managed water systems-exemplified resilience and sustainability. Conversely, extractive exploitation, often justified by short-term gains, has repeatedly led to biodiversity loss, soil degradation, and climate vulnerability. Philosophically, environmental stewardship interrogates anthropocentric paradigms, challenging the assumption that human needs automatically supersede ecological thresholds. By cultivating ecological empathy, it promotes a recognition of intrinsic value in nonhuman life and a duty of care that transcends utilitarian calculus. On a sociopolitical level, stewardship manifests through legislation, policy frameworks, and civic initiatives that prioritize environmental justice. Yet, token gestures such as symbolic tree-planting campaigns or eco-certifications without systemic reform risk being performative, masking persistent environmental inequities. Economically, environmental stewardship drives innovation in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, and circular economies. Diverse stakeholder engagement-from local communities to multinational corporations-enhances adaptive capacity and problem-solving, demonstrating that ecological responsibility and economic vitality are not mutually exclusive. In an era marked by climate crisis and rapid urbanization, the imperative to sustain ecological diversity is both urgent and complex. Stewardship, therefore, is not merely a technical practice; it is an ethical and existential orientation, underscoring humanity's intertwined fate with the natural world. SSC CGL 25/09/2025 (Shift 2)

This system operates automatically and quickly, with little or no effort. On the other hand, System 2 is the slower, more deliberate mode of thinking. It allocates attention to effortful mental activities, such as solving complex problems or evaluating logical arguments. System 2 is more methodical and rational, but it is also lazier-it prefers to endorse the intuitions of System 1 rather than question them. This division of labour works well most of the time, but it also creates predictable errors. Because System 1 is prone to biases and snap judgments, we often make decisions that are not as rational as we believe. Understanding these two systems can help us recognize when we are relying too much on intuition and when we need to engage in more deliberate thinking.

questions.question_text: person who talks too much about trivial matters. SSC CGL 14/10/2025 (Shift 3) Sol.1.(b) Palindrome a word, phrase, or sequence that reads the same backwards as forwards. Anagram a word, phrase, or name formed by rearranging the letters of another. Homonym each of two or more words having the same spelling or pronunciation but different meanings and origins. Synonym a word or phrase that means exactly or nearly the same as another word or phrase in the same language. Sol.2.(b) Austere -Practising severe self-discipline and abstention, typically for religious reasons. Hedonistic engaged in the pursuit of pleasure. Debauched -indulging in sensual pleasures to a degree considered immoral or harmful. Sybaritic fond of sensuous luxury or pleasure. Sol.3.(b) Apoplexy - a sudden, violent outburst of emotion or activity. Frenzy - wild excitement or uncontrolled activity. Tempest - a violent storm. Maelstrom -a powerful whirlpool or turbulent situation. Sol.4.(c) Nihilismthe rejection of all religious and moral principles, often in the belief that life is meaningless. Sol.5.(c) Feud a prolonged and bitter quarrel or dispute. Consensus general agreement. Amity a friendly relationship. Concord -agreement or harmony between people or groups. Sol.6.(c) Entomologist a specialist in the study of insects. Zoologist -a scientist who studies animals. Ornithologist a scientist who studies birds. Botanist a scientist who studies plants. Sol.7.(a) Testament Loquacious -a person talks excessively, often about unimportant things. Taciturn - means reserved or silent by nature. Reticent - refers to someone unwilling to speak or express their thoughts freely. - means concise and meaningful in Pithy speech or writing. Sol.8.(c) Hedonist -a person who believes that the pursuit of pleasure is the most important goal in life. Stoic - someone who endures pain or hardship without showing feelings. Cynic - a person who believes people are motivated purely by self-interest. Epicure - a person with refined taste in food and drink. Sol.9.(b) Amnesty an official pardon for people who have been convicted of political offenses. Absolution a formal release from guilt, obligation, or punishment. Reprieve -a cancellation or postponement of a punishment. Exoneration -the action of officially absolving someone from blame; vindication. Sol.10.(b) Haphephobia -an extreme or irrational fear of being touched. Atychiphobia - fear of failure. Gamophobia -fear of marriage or commitment. Thanatophobia - fear of death or dying. Sol.11.(b) Xenodochial - friendly and kind to strangers or foreigners. Misoneistic - having a hatred or fear of change or innovation. Misanthropic -disliking or distrusting humankind in general. Xylotomous -capable of cutting or boring into wood (used for certain insects). Sol.12.(b) Solipsist -A person who believes that only the self exists and that everything outside one's own mind is merely an illusion. Nihilist - denies all religious and moral principles, believing life is meaningless. Existentialist -emphasizes individual freedom and responsibility in creating meaning. Idealist -believes reality is mentally constructed or spiritual in essence. Sol.13.(b) Incendiary - A person who deliberately stirs up discord or rebellion within an organization, often to achieve personal or political ends. Iconoclast - someone who challenges or attacks established beliefs or traditions. Insubordinate - someone who refuses to obey authority, but not necessarily one who provokes rebellion. Insurrectionist - one who takes part in an OWS organized uprising against authority, but focuses on action, not provocation. Sol.14.(c) Anthology a collection of literary extracts, especially from one author. Lexicographer a person who compiles a dictionary. Bibliophile a person who loves reading and collecting books. Ennui feelings of being bored and not satisfied because nothing interesting is happening. Sol.15.(a) Extempore a speech made without any preparation. Dialogue - a conversation between two or more people. Monologue -a long speech by one person, often in a play or performance. Soliloquy - a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud when alone on stage. Sol.16.(c) Paleographer -a person who studies ancient writings and inscriptions. Archaeologist - a person who studies human history and prehistory through the excavation of sites and the analysis of artefacts and other physical remains. Epigraphist -a person who studies inscriptions, which are writings engraved on hard surfaces like stone or metal Philologist -a person who studies language in historical sources, such as literature and written records. Sol.17.(d) Esotericable to be understood by only a few people who have special knowledge or interest. Opaqueunable to be understood. Inefficientnot achieving maximum productivity. Illegiblenot clear enough to be read. Sol.18.(b) Confluence - a place where two rivers meet. Estuary - the tidal mouth of a large river, where the tide meets the stream. Delta - a triangular tract of sediment deposited at the mouth of a river, typically where it diverges into several outlets. Tributary - a river or stream flowing into a larger river or lake. Sol.19.(c) Omnipotent - having unlimited power; all-powerful. Omnipresent - present everywhere at the same time. Omniscient -knowing everything; all-knowing. Magnanimous -very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful. Sol.20.(b) Paradox - a statement that seems self-contradictory but may be true. Epigram -a short, clever, and witty saying. Aphorism -a concise statement expressing a general truth or principle. Dogma - a set of principles or beliefs laid down by an authority as unquestionable truth. Sol.21.(a) Recluse - a person who avoids human society and prefers to live alone. Renegade - a person who deserts or betrays an organization, country, or set of principles. Prodigy - a person, especially a young one, with exceptional talents or abilities. Mystic - a person who seeks spiritual truth or union with the divine through meditation or contemplation. Sol.22.(b) Quixotic - extremely idealistic, unrealistic, and impractical in pursuit of ideals. Visionary - one who thinks about or plans the future with imagination or wisdom. Sagacious -having or showing keen mental discernment and good judgment; wise. Maverick -an independent-minded person who refuses to follow accepted norms or rules. Sol.23.(d) Pacifist -a person who believes that war and violence are unjustifiable. Chauvinist -a person displaying aggressive or exaggerated patriotism. Maverick -an unorthodox or independent-minded person. Belligerent - hostile and aggressive. Sol.24.(c) Skeptic - One who finds it difficult to believe anything without proof. Credulous - having or showing too great a readiness to believe things. Agnostic - a person who believes that nothing is known or can be known of the existence or nature of God or of anything beyond material phenomena. Cynic -a person who believes that people are motivated purely by self-interest rather than acting for honourable or unselfish reasons. Sol.25.(b) Philosopher - a person who loves and seeks wisdom or knowledge. Philanthropist -a person who loves mankind and helps others, especially by giving money to good causes Philologist -a person who studies languages and their development Philatelist - a person who collects stamps Sol.26.(b) Dilettante -a person who gives opinions on something beyond their knowledge. Amateur - a person who engages in an activity for pleasure, not professionally. Novice - a beginner; someone new to a field or activity. Ignoramus -a totally ignorant or uneducated person. Sol.27.(c) Allegory a story, poem, or picture that can be interpreted to reveal a hidden meaning, typically a moral or political one. Kind -having or showing a friendly, generous, and considerate nature. Generous showing a readiness to give more of something, especially money, than is necessary or expected. Compassionate -feeling or showing sympathy and concern for others. Sol.2.(c) Frail (of a person) weak and delicate. Potentate a person with great power. Puissant one who wields great power or sway. Sovereign a supreme ruler, especially a monarch. Monarch a sovereign head of state, especially a king, queen, or emperor. Sol.3.(b) Exasperate - to irritate intensely. Placate - to make (someone) less angry or hostile. Appease - to pacify or placate (someone) by acceding to their demands. Pacify - to quell the anger, agitation, or excitement of. Conciliate -to stop (someone) from being angry or discontented. Sol.4.(b) Odorless - having no smell. Redolent -strongly smelling of something. Fragrant - having a pleasant or sweet smell. Evocative -bringing strong images, memories, or feelings to mind. Pungent - having a sharply strong taste or smell. Sol.5.(b) Permanent lasting or intended to last or remain unchanged indefinitely. Fugacious tending to disappear. Vanishingdisappear suddenly and completely. Temporarylasting for only a limited period of time. Transitory not permanent or lasting. Sol.6.(a) Philanthropist a person who seeks to promote the welfare of others, especially by the generous donation of money to good causes. Misanthrope -a person who dislikes humankind and avoids human society. Narcissist -a person who has an excessive interest in or admiration of themselves. Cynic -a person who believes that people are motivated purely by self -interest rather than acting for honourable or unselfish reasons. People-hater a person who dislikes humankind and avoids human society. Sol.7.(b) Benign gentle and kind. Pernicious having a harmful effect. Deleterious causing harm or damage. Lachrymose given to weeping. Malignant malevolent. Sol.8.(a) Sincerity the quality of being honest or genuine. Duplicity deceitfulness. Guile sly or cunning intelligence. Cunning having or showing skill in achieving one's ends by deceit or evasion. Artifice a clever or artful skill. Sol.9.(b) Harsh unpleasantly rough or jarring to the senses. questions.question_text: Select the correct homonym from Sol.76.(a) cast The phrasal verb 'cast away' means to dismiss ideas or habits. The given sentence states that we should cast away all the prejudices to live in harmony. Hence, 'cast' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.77.(d) reign 'Reign' means the period of rule of monarch. The given sentence states that during the reign of Queen Victoria, England made all-round progress. Hence, 'reign' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.78.(a) right The given sentence states that he has the right to express his thoughts. Hence, 'right' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.79.(b) their 'Their' and 'There' have similar pronunciation. Hence, 'their' is the most appropriate homophone of 'there'. Sol.80.(c) floor 'Floor' is the lower surface of a room on which one may walk. The given sentence states that the floor was decorated with candles and chocolates everywhere. Hence, 'floor' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.81.(c) heal 'Heal' means to cause (a wound, injury, or person) to become sound or healthy again. The given sentence states that the ointment will help to heal the wound. Hence, 'heal' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.82.(a) rode 'Rode' is the past form of 'ride' which means to travel by sitting on a horse, bicycle, or motorcycle. The given sentence states that he rode his bike as fast as he could to reach home. Hence, 'rode' is the most appropriate answer. Sol.83.(d) A, C 'Row' as a verb means to propel a boat by moving oars. 'In a row' means one after another without a break. The given sentence states that The rowing instructor commanded them to row in a row. Hence, 'row, row' is the most appropriate answer.
